title: Why Delhi Turns Into a Gas Chamber Every Winter (Smog Explained Simply)
description: Why does Delhi get covered in thick smog every winter? Smoke, stubble burning, traffic, a hidden lid of warm air called the inversion layer and the shape of the land all work together. This video explains it step by step, shows what PM2.5 does inside your body, and what actually protects you.
tags: how to protect from air pollution

scenes.text: Every November, Delhi wakes up inside a grey cloud. The sun looks like a pale coin. Your eyes burn, your throat feels scratchy, and the number on the screen says five hundred. What is this cloud? Where does it come from? And why does it come back every single year?

Let's start with the name. Smog is just smoke plus fog. Fog is tiny water droplets floating near the ground. Smoke is tiny bits of burnt stuff. When they mix and get trapped close to the ground, you get a thick, dirty haze that you can see, smell and taste.

But the real danger is too small to see. Scientists measure these specks as PM two point five. That means particles smaller than two and a half micrometres. A single strand of your hair is about thirty times wider. Twenty eight of them fit side by side across one hair.

To measure how dirty the air is, we use the Air Quality Index, or AQI. Zero to fifty is good. Up to one hundred is satisfactory. Above two hundred, the air is poor. And above four hundred, it is severe, which means even healthy people can fall sick.

So where do all these particles come from? Let's follow them. First stop: the farms of Punjab and Haryana. After harvesting rice, farmers have only a few weeks to clear the leftover stalks, called stubble, before planting wheat. Burning it is the cheapest and fastest way.

Every burning field sends up a column of smoke. Thousands of fields burning together make a huge smoky river. The north-west wind picks it up and carries it hundreds of kilometres, straight toward Delhi. That is why the smog gets worse right after harvest season.

But stubble is only one part of the story. Inside the city, millions of vehicles run on petrol and diesel. Their exhaust pipes release tiny soot particles and gases like nitrogen oxides. In slow, jammed traffic the engines run longer, so they release even more.

Add the factories and coal power plants, burning fuel all day. Add dust from roads and construction sites. Add garbage fires and winter heaters. And then comes Diwali, when crackers add a sudden burst of smoke and metal particles to an already heavy sky.

Now here's the twist. These pollutants exist all year, so why is winter the worst? The answer is a hidden trick of the atmosphere called a temperature inversion. Let's look at the sky from the side to understand it.

On a normal day, the ground warms the air near it. Warm air is light, so it rises, carrying the smoke high up and away. Fresh air comes in to replace it. The sky works like a chimney, constantly cleaning the city.

But on a cold winter night, the ground loses heat fast and the air near it turns cold. Higher up, a layer of warmer air sits on top. Cold air is heavy, so it stays down. And the warm air above it acts like a lid on a pot.

Everything the city releases rises a little, hits that invisible lid, and stops. There is nowhere to go. In the morning, the lid is still there, and the smoke keeps piling up, night after night. This is the inversion layer.

Wind could break the lid, but winter winds are weak. And Delhi's geography makes it worse. The city sits on flat land, far from the sea, with the Himalayas to the north. The mountains block the air from moving out, so the pollution just sits there like water in a bowl.

So there is more smoke going in, and less air going out. That is how a city turns into a gas chamber. Now let's see what it does to the one thing that cannot avoid it: your body. Come with me. We are going on a journey inside your nose.

When you breathe in, air first meets your nose. Tiny hairs and sticky mucus catch the big dust, like a doormat. Larger particles get stuck here, and you sneeze or cough them out. Your nose is a very good filter, but it has limits.

PM two point five is small enough to slip past this doormat. It travels down your windpipe, through branching tubes, all the way to the tiny air sacs of the lungs, called alveoli. You have around five hundred million of them, thin as soap bubbles.

And here is the scary part. The walls of these air sacs are so thin that oxygen passes straight into your blood. But the smallest particles can sneak across too. Once they are in the blood, they travel to the heart, the brain and everywhere else.

That is why smog does not only cause coughing. It can trigger asthma, make breathing difficult, raise the risk of heart problems, and harm children and older people the most. Children breathe faster for their size, so they take in more polluted air.

The good news: you can protect yourself. First, a mask. A simple cloth or surgical mask stops big dust, but not the tiny particles. An N95 mask has layers of special fibres that trap particles with static charge, and when it fits tightly, it blocks about ninety five percent.

Second, an air purifier with a HEPA filter. A fan pulls room air through a dense mesh of fibres that traps particles as small as point three micrometres. Keep doors and windows closed while it runs, and choose a size that fits your room.

Third, small habits help. Check the AQI before going out. Avoid jogging in the early morning, when the inversion lid is strongest and the air is the dirtiest. Keep windows closed on the worst days, and ventilate in the afternoon, when the air clears a little.

One more thing: do not trust myths. Lemon, steam and jaggery water are not proven to flush particles out of your lungs. Indoor plants are lovely, but you would need a jungle to clean a room. The science says one thing: reduce your exposure.

The real fix has to come from all of us together. Cleaner public transport, stricter rules for factories, helping farmers manage stubble without burning, and less cracker smoke. Cities like Beijing and London cleared their skies step by step, and Delhi can too.

So next time you see that grey sky, you will know the story: burning stubble, traffic, factories, an invisible lid, and a city shaped like a bowl. Understanding it is the first step to fixing it. If this helped you, subscribe, and tell me which topic you want next.
